accepted.label: One-Hot Encoding
accepted.description: One-hot encoding represents each word as a sparse vector with a 1 at the vocabulary index and zeros elsewhere, resulting in high-dimensional, inefficient representations.
coverage_criteria: Create a one-hot vector for a given word from a small vocabulary.
Explain why one-hot vectors are sparse and high-dimensional.
accepted.merge_rationale: This candidate fully covers the concept and stands alone.

accepted.label: Count-Based Text Representations and Limitations
accepted.description: Bag-of-Words and TF-IDF represent text by counting words (or n-grams) and weighting them by importance. Preprocessing steps like stemming and stop-word removal are common. These methods yield sparse vectors that ignore word context and cannot handle unknown words.
coverage_criteria: Compute Bag-of-Words and TF-IDF vectors for a small corpus.
List at least two limitations of count-based representations.
Explain the purpose of stemming and stop-word removal in text preprocessing.
accepted.merge_rationale: These candidates together describe count-based methods (BoW, TF-IDF), necessary preprocessing, and their shortcomings, forming a coherent unit that transitions into the need for dense embeddings.

accepted.label: Word Embeddings as Dense Vectors
accepted.description: Unlike sparse encodings, word embeddings are dense numerical vectors where each dimension captures latent features. They are lower-dimensional than the vocabulary and enable models to process semantic meaning efficiently.
coverage_criteria: Define word embeddings and contrast them with sparse representations.
Explain why dense vectors are more efficient than one-hot vectors.
accepted.merge_rationale: Both candidates introduce embeddings: one gives the general definition, the other focuses on density. Together they provide a complete introductory concept.

accepted.label: Semantic Similarity and Properties of Embedding Space
accepted.description: In a distributional framework, words are similar if they share similar contexts. Embedding vectors place these words in a space where distance (e.g., cosine) reflects similarity. Well‑trained embeddings also exhibit clustering of related words and support analogical reasoning (e.g., king - man + woman ≈ queen).
coverage_criteria: Explain how word similarity is defined by context rather than spelling.
Given a 2D plot, identify which words are most similar based on distance.
Describe the analogy property of ideal embeddings with an example.
accepted.merge_rationale: These three candidates build a narrative from contextual similarity to distance‑based similarity and finally the desired properties of clustering and analogies, making a cohesive teachable segment.

accepted.label: Training a Custom Embedding Layer
accepted.description: A neural network can include an embedding layer initialized randomly and trained end‑to‑end for a specific task, producing specialized word representations. This requires large amounts of data.
coverage_criteria: Describe how a custom embedding layer is trained within a model.
State one advantage and one disadvantage of training embeddings from scratch.
accepted.merge_rationale: The candidate covers the method succinctly and stands alone.

accepted.label: Word2vec: CBOW and Skip‑gram Architectures
accepted.description: Word2vec learns embeddings by training a shallow neural network on a prediction task: Continuous Bag‑of‑Words (CBOW) predicts a target word from context, while Skip‑gram predicts context words from a target word.
coverage_criteria: Differentiate CBOW and Skip‑gram and state what each predicts.
Explain how Word2vec creates dense word vectors from unlabeled text.
accepted.merge_rationale: This candidate describes both architectures and forms a single well‑defined technique.

accepted.label: GloVe: Global Vectors for Word Representation
accepted.description: GloVe improves on Word2vec by leveraging a word co‑occurrence matrix, training vectors such that their dot product approximates the log of co‑occurrence probability, thereby incorporating global corpus statistics.
coverage_criteria: Explain how GloVe differs from Word2vec regarding global information.
Describe the role of the co‑occurrence matrix in GloVe.
accepted.merge_rationale: This candidate specifically addresses GloVe and its unique mechanism; no other candidates cover it.

accepted.label: fastText: Subword Embeddings
accepted.description: fastText represents each word as the sum of its character n‑gram embeddings, allowing it to build vectors for out‑of‑vocabulary words and handle morphologically rich languages.
coverage_criteria: Explain how fastText’s subword approach addresses the out‑of‑vocabulary problem.
Describe the difference between Word2vec and fastText regarding word representation.
accepted.merge_rationale: This candidate fully covers the fastText method and its benefits.

accepted.label: ELMo: Contextualized Word Embeddings
accepted.description: ELMo uses a bidirectional LSTM to produce word vectors that depend on the entire input sentence, allowing the same word to have different representations in different contexts (e.g., homonyms).
coverage_criteria: Explain why ELMo provides different embeddings for the same word in different sentences.
Describe the advantage of context‑dependent over static word embeddings.
accepted.merge_rationale: This candidate is the only one covering ELMo and stands alone.

accepted.label: Using Pre‑trained Word Embeddings
accepted.description: Pre‑trained word vectors can be used in two ways: as static features (fixed during downstream training) or fine‑tuned (adjusted to the task). The Gensim library provides convenient access to pre‑trained models (Word2vec, GloVe, fastText) and similarity operations.
coverage_criteria: List and describe the two modes of using pre‑trained embeddings.
Write code to load a pre‑trained model from Gensim and find similar words.
accepted.merge_rationale: c014 covers the theoretical usage modes, while c015 demonstrates a practical tool (Gensim) for working with pre‑trained embeddings; together they form a complete practical concept.

accepted.label: TF-IDF Definition and Computation
accepted.description: TF-IDF is a statistical measure of word relevance in a document corpus, computed as the product of Term Frequency (TF) and Inverse Document Frequency (IDF). TF measures how often a term appears in a document, normalized by document length. IDF measures how rare a term is across the corpus, using log(N/df). The product gives a weight that highlights terms that are frequent in a specific document but rare overall, yielding document feature vectors.
coverage_criteria: Define TF-IDF and its purpose.
Calculate TF, IDF, and TF-IDF for a given term in a small corpus.
accepted.merge_rationale: All candidates describe the same core idea: the definition, components, and arithmetic of TF-IDF.

accepted.label: TF-IDF Output: Document Vectors and Applications
accepted.description: After computing TF-IDF for all terms, each document is represented as a weighted term vector, where high weights indicate discriminative terms. These document vectors are used in data mining tasks such as classification, clustering, and information retrieval, especially document search.
coverage_criteria: Explain how TF-IDF transforms documents into feature vectors.
List at least three applications of TF-IDF in text analysis.
accepted.merge_rationale: All candidates cover the output representation and practical uses of TF-IDF.

accepted.label: TF-IDF Discriminative Power and Comparison with Bag of Words
accepted.description: TF-IDF assigns higher weights to terms that appear frequently in a specific document but rarely across the corpus, making them discriminative features. A term that appears in every document gets IDF=0 and thus TF-IDF=0, meaning it has no discriminative power. This contrasts with Bag of Words, which merely counts occurrences and does not differentiate important terms from common ones.
coverage_criteria: Explain why a word with IDF=0 is not useful for distinguishing documents.
Describe the key difference between Bag of Words and TF-IDF.
accepted.merge_rationale: Both candidates address the weighting behavior of TF-IDF and its advantage over simple counts, covering the special case of zero IDF.

accepted.label: Implementing TF-IDF with Scikit-learn: TfidfVectorizer and Preprocessing
accepted.description: In Python, TF-IDF can be computed using TfidfVectorizer from sklearn. This requires preparing text by splitting into documents (e.g., splitlines) and optionally removing stopwords using NLTK's stopwords list, passed to the stop_words parameter. The fit_transform method returns a TF-IDF matrix.
coverage_criteria: Write code to import TfidfVectorizer, include stopwords from NLTK, and fit_transform a list of documents.
accepted.merge_rationale: All candidates describe practical steps for implementing TF-IDF in Python with scikit-learn: using the vectorizer, stopword removal, and document splitting.

accepted.label: NLP Vocabulary: Document, Body, Dictionary, Topic
accepted.description: In NLP, a document is a single data instance (e.g., a paragraph, tweet). The body (or corpus) is the collection of all documents. The dictionary is the set of all unique words occurring in at least one document. A topic is a collection of co-occurring words that represent a theme.
coverage_criteria: Define the terms document, body (corpus), dictionary, and topic in NLP.
accepted.merge_rationale: This candidate introduces the fundamental NLP vocabulary needed for understanding text representation methods.

accepted.label: Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA) Definition
accepted.description: LSA is an unsupervised NLP technique that discovers latent topics in a corpus by applying dimensionality reduction (via SVD) to the document-term matrix, yielding lower-dimensional encodings of documents as combinations of topics.
coverage_criteria: Explain what LSA is and its purpose in text analysis.
accepted.merge_rationale: This candidate provides the core definition of LSA.

accepted.label: Document-Term Matrix in LSA
accepted.description: A document-term matrix is a representation where rows correspond to documents, columns to dictionary words, and cells indicate word presence or frequency. It serves as the input to SVD in LSA.
coverage_criteria: Describe the structure of a document-term matrix.
accepted.merge_rationale: This candidate explains the matrix representation that LSA builds upon.

accepted.label: Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) in LSA
accepted.description: In LSA, Singular Value Decomposition is applied to the document-term matrix to reduce its dimensionality and extract latent topics, analogous to PCA. This transforms the high-dimensional word space into a lower-dimensional topic space.
coverage_criteria: State the role of SVD in LSA and its analogy to PCA.
accepted.merge_rationale: This candidate focuses on the SVD step that gives LSA its latent topic discovery capability.
